Ternate chromis (Chromis ternatensis) is a small-bodied damselfish inhabiting coral reef environments throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific. Field surveys in the Moluccas indicate that newly hatched prolarvae emerge from demersal eggs after an incubation period of approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days] when water temperatures are stable at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. The wet weight at birth, calculated from the typical egg diameter of one millimeter, is an extremely modest 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value that reflects the planktonic larval strategy common among pomacentrids. This tiny initial mass places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum for newly hatched coral-reef fishes, comparable to other small-bodied damselfishes that produce pelagic larvae with limited endogenous reserves. The lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva depends entirely on its yolk nutrients during the first few days following eclosion, a critical window during which the chorionate embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis and swim bladder inflation before the onset of exogenous feeding.

As individuals progress through the yolk-sac larval stage, the depletion of lipid stores drives a substantial increase in body length. By the time young-of-year reach the juvenile phase, growth trajectories become increasingly determinate, with adults typically attaining a maximum standard length of 10.5 centimeters [Li = 10.5 centimeters]. This ultimate body size is relatively modest among the damselfishes of the genus Chromis, which includes species that can exceed 15 centimeters in total length. The species exhibits a moderate growth coefficient and reaches puberty at a standard length of approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters], a developmental milestone that signals the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Achieving this threshold size typically requires several months of sustained feeding on zooplankton in the water column, as the benthic juvenile forages actively among coral branches and rock crevices.

At the attainment of reproductive maturity, the wet weight of a pubertal individual averages around 3 grams [Wwp = around 3 grams], a body mass that reflects the energetic investments already made in somatic tissue and the initiation of vitellogenesis. The maximum reported wet weight for fully grown adults, based on length-weight relationships derived from field-caught specimens, is 29.1 grams [Wwi = 29.1 grams], a figure consistent with the allometric scaling observed across congeners. Females at this asymptotic size carry substantial lipid reserves that support the production of multiple clutches during a single breeding season. Under the stable thermal regime characteristic of their equatorial habitat, maintained at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate of Chromis ternatensis has been estimated from spawning observations at 200 eggs per day [Ri = 200 eggs per day], a value derived from intensive monitoring of nesting behavior in the closely related Chromis chromis but consistent with the life-history patterns observed in this species.

Reproductive output in Ternate chromis is partitioned into distinct spawning events rather than continuous egg release. Field observations indicate that gravid individuals typically produce a clutch of approximately 200 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 200 eggs per spawning event], with the frequency of these events reaching a peak of one spawning per day [F_R_i = one spawning per day] during the height of the breeding season at the same water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This iteroparous strategy, characterized by high fecundity and multiple daily reproductive bouts, is energetically demanding and appears to be constrained by prey availability and intraspecific competition for nesting sites. The age at first reproduction, measured from the moment of egg hatching, occurs relatively early in the species' life cycle, with many individuals initiating their first breeding efforts within the first year following larval metamorphosis and benthic settlement on the reef.

Longevity records for Chromis ternatensis in the wild suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] under the stable thermal conditions of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] typical of its tropical habitat. This lifespan is comparable to other small-bodied demersal-spawning pomacentrids, though it remains significantly shorter than some larger congeners that may persist for over a decade. As individuals approach senescence, age-related declines in swimming performance and foraging efficiency become apparent, contributing to natural mortality through predation and metabolic deterioration. The relatively early sexual maturation at a standard length of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm] allows individuals to enter the breeding population within their first year, a life-history trait that buffers against the high and unpredictable mortality rates typical of coral reef environments, where small body size and high fecundity compensate for relatively brief reproductive tenure.
